misconceptions.description: The learner treats a Riemann sum as an operation on the list of function values alone, so the partition widths play no role and every subinterval is implicitly treated alike.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Present a table whose inputs are unevenly spaced and ask for the value of one term of the sum together with its units.
misconceptions.name: A Riemann sum is a sum of the listed values

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the left, right, and midpoint choices as interchangeable labels rather than as different sample points that give different sums.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the left and the right sum on the same monotone table and ask whether the two values must agree.
misconceptions.name: The endpoint convention is cosmetic

misconceptions.description: The learner treats a Riemann sum as the value of the definite integral rather than as an approximation whose error has a direction.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask whether the reported sum is larger or smaller than the integral and how the student knows.
misconceptions.name: Riemann sums are exact

misconceptions.description: The learner averages across the entire interval rather than forming a separate trapezoid on each subinterval.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the area of the single trapezoid on the first subinterval.
misconceptions.name: A trapezoid is a rectangle at the average height of the whole interval

misconceptions.description: The learner applies one monotonicity rule to every approximation method, so concavity never enters the reasoning.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Give an increasing concave down rate and ask for the direction of a trapezoidal estimate and of a left sum separately.
misconceptions.name: Approximation direction follows from increase or decrease alone

misconceptions.description: The learner does not separate whether a function rises from whether it bends upward, so the two justifications are exchanged freely.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to sketch a decreasing concave up curve.
misconceptions.name: Concavity and monotonicity are the same property

misconceptions.description: The learner attaches every question about the accumulation function to the visible features of the plotted integrand, so extrema and inflection points are read off the wrong curve.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to label the plotted curve and the accumulation function separately before answering.
misconceptions.name: The plotted curve is the function under discussion

misconceptions.description: The learner uses the zeros of f for every feature of g, so both extrema and inflection points are placed at the same inputs.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask where g has extrema and where g has inflection points on the same graph and compare the two lists.
misconceptions.name: A zero of the integrand is a general turning feature of the accumulation function

misconceptions.description: The learner believes that naming the defining property, such as g changing concavity, answers a request for a reason, without connecting the claim to the supplied representation.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what feature of the given graph makes the stated claim true.
misconceptions.name: Restating a definition counts as a reason

misconceptions.description: The learner treats a first or second derivative test at one input as sufficient for an absolute extremum on a closed interval.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask whether the endpoints can beat the interior candidate and how that is checked.
misconceptions.name: A relative extremum test settles an absolute extremum

misconceptions.description: The learner reproduces area formulas for triangles, trapezoids, and semicircles without the halving factor.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the area of a single semicircle of a stated radius.
misconceptions.name: Area formulas are recalled without their fractional factors

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the definite integral as the total area of the region between the graph and the axis, with no sign attached to regions below the axis.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the integral of a rate that is negative on the whole interval.
misconceptions.name: The definite integral measures unsigned area

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the accumulated change as the value of the quantity itself, so the initial condition has no role.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Give a rate and two different initial values and ask for the value at the later input in each case.
misconceptions.name: The integral of a rate is the amount of the quantity

misconceptions.description: The learner does not separate the integral from the integral divided by the interval length, so the two expressions are described and computed interchangeably.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Show both expressions side by side and ask for the units of each.
misconceptions.name: Average value and accumulated amount are the same quantity

misconceptions.description: The learner applies a difference quotient wherever the word average appears, so an average value request is answered with a slope.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask which of the two answers has the units of the function and which has the units of a rate.
misconceptions.name: Average of a function and average rate of change are the same quantity

misconceptions.description: The learner treats u as a shorthand label rather than a change of variable, so limits of integration and differentials carry over unchanged.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what the lower limit becomes after the substitution and why.
misconceptions.name: Substitution renames a variable without changing the problem

misconceptions.description: The learner selects substitution from the presence of an inner function alone, without checking that its derivative is present.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to write du and point to it inside the integrand.
misconceptions.name: A composite integrand guarantees that substitution applies

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the antiderivative as unique, so the arbitrary constant is decoration rather than part of the answer.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to name two different functions with the same given derivative.
misconceptions.name: An antiderivative is a single function

misconceptions.description: The learner extends the sum rule to products, so each factor is antidifferentiated on its own.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to differentiate the proposed product and compare with the integrand.
misconceptions.name: Antidifferentiation distributes across a product

misconceptions.description: The learner treats infinity as an endpoint value rather than as a limiting process, so improper integrals are evaluated by substitution.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to write the improper integral as a limit before antidifferentiating.
misconceptions.name: Infinity is a number that can be substituted

misconceptions.description: The learner concludes convergence from the integrand approaching zero, so the limit is never examined.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Compare the integrals of one over x and one over x squared on the same infinite interval.
misconceptions.name: Every improper integral of a decaying integrand converges

misconceptions.description: The learner selects a technique from a visual resemblance to a worked example rather than from the structural precondition the technique requires.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to state the condition the chosen technique requires and to point to it in the integrand.
misconceptions.name: Technique choice follows the surface look of the integrand

misconceptions.description: The learner applies the theorem as a fixed template regardless of what the upper limit is.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the derivative of the upper limit on its own before the theorem is applied.
misconceptions.name: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus part one has no chain rule

misconceptions.description: The learner does not distinguish the bound variable inside the integral from the variable in the upper limit.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask whether changing the letter of the variable of integration changes the function.
misconceptions.name: The variable of integration is the independent variable

misconceptions.description: The learner omits the interval or the units because the quantity has been identified.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what would change in the sentence if the interval were different.
misconceptions.name: An interpretation is complete once the quantity is named

misconceptions.description: The learner applies F(b) minus F(a) without checking that the integrand is continuous on the interval.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Give an integrand with a jump inside the interval and ask whether the theorem applies directly.
misconceptions.name: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus part two needs no hypotheses
